title: Decimal(0.1) is not Decimal("0.1") - switching to Decimal doesn't fix the bug if you build it from a float
assumption: Wrapping a problematic float in decimal.Decimal() makes it exact, regardless of how the Decimal was constructed.

input.description: A developer who hits a float rounding bug in money code and "fixes" it by calling Decimal() on an existing float variable, instead of re-reading the original value as a string.

what_goes_wrong: `Decimal(0.1)` prints as `Decimal('0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625')` - Decimal faithfully captured the float's actual binary value, not the clean decimal 0.1 - while `Decimal("0.1")` is exactly `Decimal('0.1')`. The two are unequal, so money code that parses a string to a float and only then wraps it in Decimal has already lost precision before Decimal ever runs.
why: `decimal.Decimal` is exact in base 10, but it can only be as exact as the input it's given. Passed a `float`, the constructor reads out that float's true (imprecise) IEEE-754 double value in full and stores exactly that - it cannot recover the "0.1" a human typed, because by the time it's a float, that information is already gone. Passed a `str`, it parses the decimal digits directly with no binary detour, so it is exact. JavaScript has no built-in decimal type (TC39's Decimal proposal is not part of the language), but the JavaScript repro shows the same fact from the other side: the Number written as 0.1 holds exactly 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625, so any decimal library constructed from that Number rather than from the string "0.1" starts from the wrong value.

repros.code:
from decimal import Decimal
a = Decimal(0.1)
b = Decimal("0.1")
print(a)
print(b)
print(a == b)
print(Decimal(0.1) + Decimal(0.2) == Decimal("0.3"))
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"))

fix: Always construct Decimal (or any exact money type) from the original string the user typed or the database stored - never from a float that has already rounded the value. If a float is all you have, treat it as already-corrupted and document the tolerance you're accepting.

test_cases.note: A their_make_decimal(value) helper should document whether it accepts floats at all; if it does, Decimal(0.1) != Decimal("0.1") must not be silently assumed equal downstream.
